\chapter{Salt, Honey, Milk, Egg, Fish}
\label{ch:la-mensa}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five things on a Latin table, and I can use Grimm's Law to tell an inherited English cousin from a borrowed Latin loan.}

The fifth word of the group, taken apart against the four before it.

\section[sāl, salis]{sāl — a cousin of English salt, and the word a Roman soldier's salary was named for}

\label{lesson:LA-C47-sal}



\begin{quote}
A new group of five words begins here. Nothing is assumed but the alphabet you already read.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{sāl} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{salt}.\textquotedblright{}

A \textbf{cousin}: Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*séh\textsubscript{2}ls}} gave Latin \emph{sāl} and Germanic \emph{saltom}, which is English \textbf{salt}. And then Latin lent the same root back into English several more times, all through food.

A \textbf{salad} is \emph{herba salāta}, \textbf{salted} greens. A \textbf{sauce} is \emph{salsa}, the salted thing — and Spanish \textbf{salsa} is the very same word, arriving by a different road. A \textbf{sausage} is \emph{salsīcia}, salted meat. Four English food words, one Latin root.

Then \textbf{salary}. Latin \emph{salārium} was money paid to Roman soldiers, and the ancient explanation — that it was an allowance \emph{for salt} — is what Pliny reports. \textbf{Treat it as the standard account rather than as settled fact}: no document actually records soldiers being paid in salt, and some historians think \emph{salārium} simply meant a ration allowance generally. The word is certainly from \emph{sāl}. What the money bought is less certain than the story suggests.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sāl, salis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is English \emph{salt} a cousin or a loan? (\textbf{A cousin}.) Name three loans from the same root. (\textbf{Salad}, \textbf{sauce}, \textbf{sausage}, \textbf{salsa}.) And how solid is the salary story? (\textbf{Standard, not proven} — the word is from \emph{sāl}, the salt payment is Pliny's account.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mel, mellis]{mel — the root of mellifluous and marmalade, and of molasses by way of Portuguese}

\label{lesson:LA-C47-mel}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{mel} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{honey}.\textquotedblright{}

Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*melit-}}, and it is one of those roots that turns up in languages that otherwise share very little — Greek \emph{meli}, Hittite \emph{milit}, and Latin \emph{mel}, all honey.

Something \textbf{mellifluous} is \emph{mel} plus \emph{fluere}, \textbf{flowing with honey} — used of a voice. \textbf{Mellow} is probably from the same family, though the road is not clean.

Two food words came in through Portuguese, which is why they look nothing alike. \textbf{Marmalade} is \emph{marmelada}, a quince paste — Portuguese \emph{marmelo}, \textquotedblleft{}quince,\textquotedblright{} from Greek \emph{melimēlon}, a \textbf{honey-apple}. And \textbf{molasses} is Portuguese \emph{melaço}, the honey-like residue left when sugar is refined.

English \textbf{honey} itself is Germanic and comes from a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}golden.\textquotedblright{} Unrelated — a different language naming the same substance by a different property.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mel, mellis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{mellifluous} literally say? (\textbf{Flowing with honey}.) Which two food words came through Portuguese? (\textbf{Marmalade}, \textbf{molasses}.) And is English \emph{honey} related? (\textbf{No} — Germanic, from a root meaning golden.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lac, lactis]{lac — the root of lactose, lettuce and, at one remove, of the Milky Way itself}

\label{lesson:LA-C47-lac}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{lac} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{milk}.\textquotedblright{} The stem is \emph{lact-}, which is where every English relative comes from.

\textbf{Lactose} is milk sugar; \textbf{lactic} acid is named from souring milk; to \textbf{lactate} is to produce it.

Then a word nobody expects. \textbf{Lettuce} is Latin \emph{\textbf{lactūca}} — \textquotedblleft{}the \textbf{milky} one,\textquotedblright{} named for the white sap that bleeds from a cut lettuce stem. Pick one and you can watch the etymology happen.

And the Greek sibling is \emph{gala}, stem \emph{galakt-}, also \textquotedblleft{}milk.\textquotedblright{} The Greeks called the band of light across the night sky the \emph{galaxías kúklos}, the \textbf{milky circle} — which Latin rendered as \emph{via lactea} and English as the \textbf{Milky Way}. So \textbf{galaxy} and \textbf{lactose} are the same word, and the Milky Way is a translation.

You met \emph{stēlla} and \emph{lūna} a moment ago. This is the sky they are in.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lac, lactis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{lettuce} named for? (Its \textbf{milky} sap.) What does \textbf{galaxy} mean? (\textbf{Milky} — the same root, through Greek.) And what is the \textbf{Milky Way} a translation of? (Greek \emph{galaxías}, Latin \emph{via lactea}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ōvum, ōvī]{ōvum — a cousin of English egg, with two sound changes that hide the relationship completely}

\label{lesson:LA-C47-ovum}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{ōvum} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{an egg}.\textquotedblright{}

\emph{Ōvum} and \textbf{egg} are cousins — the same Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*h\textsubscript{2}ōwyóm}} — and they look nothing like each other, which makes this a good place to see how much sound change can hide.

The loans are transparent: something \textbf{oval} is egg-shaped, an \textbf{ovary} is where eggs are made, \textbf{ovulation} is their release.

The inherited word had a rougher time. Old English had \emph{æg}, and it was losing ground when Norse settlers brought their own form, \emph{egg}. For a while both were in use — Caxton complained in 1490 that a merchant asking for \emph{eggys} in Kent was not understood, because there they said \emph{eyren}. The Norse form won, and the native English one vanished.

So the everyday word is a \textbf{Viking} word that replaced a cousin of itself, and the learned words came from Latin. English is full of this.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ōvum, ōvī}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Are \emph{ōvum} and \emph{egg} related? (\textbf{Yes} — cousins, heavily disguised.) What was the native English word? (\emph{\textbf{Æg}}, plural \emph{eyren}.) And why do we say \emph{egg}? (It is the \textbf{Norse} form, and it won.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[piscis, piscis]{piscis — and the single clearest demonstration in this book of the sound law linking Latin to English}

\label{lesson:LA-C47-piscis}



\begin{quote}
Recall the previous word in this chapter before adding another.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{piscis} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{a fish}.\textquotedblright{}

Keep this word. It is the cleanest single demonstration in this book of how a Latin word and an English one can be the same word.

Latin \emph{\textbf{p}}-\emph{iscis}. English \emph{\textbf{f}}-\emph{ish}. Same word.

The change is not random. Around two thousand years ago the Germanic branch shifted every inherited \textbf{p} to \textbf{f}, and it did so \emph{without exception}. That is \textbf{Grimm's Law}, and you have already been shown its results without being told the name:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pater} $\to$ \textbf{father}
  \item \emph{pēs}, \emph{pedis} $\to$ \textbf{foot}
  \item \emph{piscis} $\to$ \textbf{fish}
\end{itemize}

Three pairs, one rule. Once you have it, you can run it yourself: Latin \emph{plēnus} against English \textbf{full}, Latin \emph{prō} against \textbf{for}.

The loans came separately and kept the \emph{p}: \textbf{Pisces} the constellation, something \textbf{piscine}, a \textbf{piscina}. So English holds both the inherited form and the borrowed one, and now you can tell which is which by looking at a single letter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{piscis, piscis}
  \item every word this chapter has given you so far, in order
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sound does Latin \emph{p} correspond to in inherited English words? (\textbf{F} — Grimm's Law.) Give two more pairs. (\emph{Pater}/\textbf{father}, \emph{pēs}/\textbf{foot}.) And why does \textbf{Pisces} keep its \emph{p}? (It is a \textbf{loan}, not inherited.)
\end{tcolorbox}
